items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to find the equation of the tangent line to the ellipse [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1] at the point [MATH: P(3,1).]

Content:
To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Content:
Let's start by defining

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.]

Content:
Then, the given ellipse is the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)=1.]

Content:
Now, we know that [MATH: \nabla \! f(3,1)] is a vector that's normal to the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)= 1] at [MATH: P(3,1).] So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at [MATH: P.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/47a27df4d774c2c1660a300d2b780714]

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: (x,y)] is any point on that tangent line. Then [MATH: \mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle] is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So [MATH: \mathbf v] must be also orthogonal to [MATH: \nabla f(3,1),] and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.]

Content:
Now, computing [MATH: \nabla\! f] and evaluating it at the point [MATH: P(3,1),] we have

Content:
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= ⟨(x)/(6), (y)/(2)⟩; ∇f(3, 1)|= ⟨(1)/(2), (1)/(2)⟩.]

Content:
Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∇f(3, 1) ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 1⟩|= 0; ⟨(1)/(2), (1)/(2)⟩ ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 1⟩|= 0; (1)/(2)(x − 3) + (1)/(2)(y − 1)|= 0; (x − 3) + (y − 1)|= 0; x + y − 4|= 0]

Content:
Let [MATH: f(x,y)] be a function that's continuously differentiable at the point [MATH: P(x_0,y_0).] If [MATH: \nabla f(x_0, y_0)] is not the zero vector, then it is orthogonal to the tangent line to the level curve

at the point [MATH: P.] The equation of the tangent can then be written as

sections.readable_text: Given the function [MATH: f(x,y) = 6x^2+2y^2 - 2xy^2,] find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where [MATH: (x,y) = (3,3).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve [MATH: f(x,y) = k] at the point [MATH: (x_0,y_0)] can be expressed as

[MATH: \nabla f(x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0 \rangle = 0.]

First, we find the gradient of [MATH: f(x,y)] and evaluate it at [MATH: (x,y) = (3,3)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = (∂)/(∂x)(6x^{2} + 2y^{2} − 2xy^{2})i + (∂)/(∂y)(6x^{2} + 2y^{2} − 2xy^{2})j; = (12x − 2y^{2})i + (4y − 4xy)j; ∇f(3, 3)|= (12(3) − 2(3)^{2})i + (4(3) − 4(3)(3))j; = 18i − 24j; = ⟨18, − 24⟩]

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the level curve that passes through the point [MATH: (x_0,y_0)=(3,3)] can be written as [MATH: ∇f(x_{0}, y_{0}) ⋅ ⟨x − x_{0}, y − y_{0}⟩|= 0; ∇f(3, 3) ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 3⟩|= 0; ⟨18, − 24⟩ ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 3⟩|= 0.]

We can leave our answer in this form. Or, if we want to leave our final answer in Cartesian form, we expand the dot product and simplify:

[MATH: 18(x − 3) − 24(y − 3)|= 0; 18x − 24y + 18|= 0; 3x − 4y + 3|= 0]

Content:
Given a level curve [MATH: f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),] a tangent vector is

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf t(x_0,y_0) = f_y(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf j.]

Content:
To understand why the above vector is tangent to the level curve, first recall that the gradient vector [MATH: \nabla f(x_0,y_0)] is normal to the level curve. Now, by computing the dot product, we see that the vector [MATH: \mathbf t] is orthogonal to the gradient vector [MATH: \nabla\! f{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∇f ⋅ t|= (f_{x}i + f_{y}j) ⋅ (f_{y}i − f_{x}j); = f_{x}f_{y} − f_{y}f_{x}; = 0]

Content:
Consequently, [MATH: \mathbf t] is tangent to the level curve.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, if we set [MATH: f(x,y) = x^2-3xy+4y,] our curve can be viewed as the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)=2.]

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point [MATH: (1,1)] can be computed as follows: [MATH: \mathbf t(1,1) = f_y(1,1) \ \mathbf i - f_x(1,1) \ \mathbf j]

So, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf t(x,y)] and evaluate it at [MATH: (1,1)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: t(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − 3xy + 4y)i − (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − 3xy + 4y)j; = (− 3x + 4)i − (2x − 3y)j; t(1, 1)|= (− 3(1) + 4)i − (2(1) − 3(1))j; = 1i − (− 1)j; = i + j]

Therefore, our tangent vector is [MATH: \mathbf i +\mathbf j,] as shown in the diagram below.

items.title: Finding the Points on a Curve at which the Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to a Given Vector

sections.normalized_html: At which points on the curve [MATH: 6xy+3y^2 =7+ y - 3x^2] is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{j}?]
sections.readable_text: At which points on the curve [MATH: 6xy+3y^2 =7+ y - 3x^2] is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{j}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we bring all variables to one side: [MATH: 6xy + 3y^{2}|= 7 + y − 3x^{2}; 6xy + 3y^{2} − y + 3x^{2}|= 7]

If we set [MATH: f(x,y) = 6xy+3y^2 - y + 3x^2 ,] our curve can be viewed as the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)=7.]

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows: [MATH: \mathbf t(x,y) = f_y(x,y) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x,y) \ \mathbf j]

So, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf t(x,y)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: t(x, y)|= f_{y}(x, y)i − f_{x}(x, y)j; = (∂)/(∂y)(6xy + 3y^{2} − y + 3x^{2})i − (∂)/(∂x)(6xy + 3y^{2} − y + 3x^{2})j; = (6x + 6y − 1)i − (6y + 6x)j]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to find the equation of the tangent line to the ellipse [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1] at the point [MATH: P(3,1).]

Content:
To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Content:
Let's start by defining

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.]

Content:
Then, the given ellipse is the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)=1.]

Content:
Now, we know that [MATH: \nabla \! f(3,1)] is a vector that's normal to the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)= 1] at [MATH: P(3,1).] So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at [MATH: P.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/47a27df4d774c2c1660a300d2b780714]

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: (x,y)] is any point on that tangent line. Then [MATH: \mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle] is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So [MATH: \mathbf v] must be also orthogonal to [MATH: \nabla f(3,1),] and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.]

Content:
Now, computing [MATH: \nabla\! f] and evaluating it at the point [MATH: P(3,1),] we have

Content:
[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= ⟨(x)/(6), (y)/(2)⟩; ∇f(3, 1)|= ⟨(1)/(2), (1)/(2)⟩.]

Content:
Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∇f(3, 1) ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 1⟩|= 0; ⟨(1)/(2), (1)/(2)⟩ ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 1⟩|= 0; (1)/(2)(x − 3) + (1)/(2)(y − 1)|= 0; (x − 3) + (y − 1)|= 0; x + y − 4|= 0]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Tangent Line to a Level Curve

Content:
Now, let's state the previous result more generally.

Content:
Let [MATH: f(x,y)] be a function that's continuously differentiable at the point [MATH: P(x_0,y_0).] If [MATH: \nabla f(x_0, y_0)] is not the zero vector, then it is orthogonal to the tangent line to the level curve

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y)= f(x_0,y_0)]

Content:
at the point [MATH: P.] The equation of the tangent can then be written as

Content:
[MATH: \nabla\! f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle = 0.]

Content:
Writing this explicitly, we get

Content:
[MATH: f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0) = 0.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Tangent Line to a Level Curve

Example Prompt:
Given the function [MATH: f(x,y) = 6x^2+2y^2 - 2xy^2,] find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where [MATH: (x,y) = (3,3).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equation of the tangent line to the level curve [MATH: f(x,y) = k] at the point [MATH: (x_0,y_0)] can be expressed as

[MATH: \nabla f(x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0 \rangle = 0.]

First, we find the gradient of [MATH: f(x,y)] and evaluate it at [MATH: (x,y) = (3,3)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ∇f(x, y)|= f_{x}(x, y)i + f_{y}(x, y)j; = (∂)/(∂x)(6x^{2} + 2y^{2} − 2xy^{2})i + (∂)/(∂y)(6x^{2} + 2y^{2} − 2xy^{2})j; = (12x − 2y^{2})i + (4y − 4xy)j; ∇f(3, 3)|= (12(3) − 2(3)^{2})i + (4(3) − 4(3)(3))j; = 18i − 24j; = ⟨18, − 24⟩]

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the level curve that passes through the point [MATH: (x_0,y_0)=(3,3)] can be written as
[MATH: ∇f(x_{0}, y_{0}) ⋅ ⟨x − x_{0}, y − y_{0}⟩|= 0; ∇f(3, 3) ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 3⟩|= 0; ⟨18, − 24⟩ ⋅ ⟨x − 3, y − 3⟩|= 0.]

We can leave our answer in this form. Or, if we want to leave our final answer in Cartesian form, we expand the dot product and simplify:

[MATH: 18(x − 3) − 24(y − 3)|= 0; 18x − 24y + 18|= 0; 3x − 4y + 3|= 0]

[IMG: /graphics/c5004ab213a6d5c7a2ffee17af5d78e1]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve

Content:
Given a level curve [MATH: f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),] a tangent vector is

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf t(x_0,y_0) = f_y(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x_0,y_0) \ \mathbf j.]

Content:
To understand why the above vector is tangent to the level curve, first recall that the gradient vector [MATH: \nabla f(x_0,y_0)] is normal to the level curve. Now, by computing the dot product, we see that the vector [MATH: \mathbf t] is orthogonal to the gradient vector [MATH: \nabla\! f{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∇f ⋅ t|= (f_{x}i + f_{y}j) ⋅ (f_{y}i − f_{x}j); = f_{x}f_{y} − f_{y}f_{x}; = 0]

Content:
Consequently, [MATH: \mathbf t] is tangent to the level curve.

---

Item 7 — Example: Finding a Tangent Vector to a Plane Curve

Example Prompt:
Consider the plane curve [MATH: x^2-3xy+4y=2.] Find a tangent vector to the curve at the point [MATH: (1,1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, if we set [MATH: f(x,y) = x^2-3xy+4y,] our curve can be viewed as the level curve [MATH: f(x,y)=2.]

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point [MATH: (1,1)] can be computed as follows:
[MATH: \mathbf t(1,1) = f_y(1,1) \ \mathbf i - f_x(1,1) \ \mathbf j]

So, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf t(x,y)] and evaluate it at [MATH: (1,1)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: t(x, y)|= (∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − 3xy + 4y)i − (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − 3xy + 4y)j; = (− 3x + 4)i − (2x − 3y)j; t(1, 1)|= (− 3(1) + 4)i − (2(1) − 3(1))j; = 1i − (− 1)j; = i + j]

Therefore, our tangent vector is [MATH: \mathbf i +\mathbf j,] as shown in the diagram below.
